intro.text: AI assistants can ship services on plain HTTP, leave admin consoles and AI tools on default credentials, and keep default settings unless told otherwise. SecureConfig gives your assistant short, copy-ready guides that make the secure option the default at each deployment decision. Guides include checks your assistant runs and reports, including what it could not verify.

value.text: An AI assistant that sets up a service does not always close every open door unless it is told to: encryption left off, default credentials for logins, factory settings kept. SecureConfig gives it a guide for each of those decisions, drawn from the vendors' documentation and [free to use under CC0](/license/), so the secure setting goes in the first time. Guides include checks that report what passed, what failed, and what could not be verified. The checklist's steps are reasoned from documented vendor behaviour, with no deployment run recorded, and most guides record the versions they were written against.

always.text: A skill loads when its description matches the task. To have the rules loaded with your project instructions, paste [plugin/always-on.md](plugin/always-on.md), the skill's rules for every deployment and 1 line pointing at the skill, into your project's `CLAUDE.md`, which Claude Code reads as project instructions at the start of a session; the [memory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) page lists the settings that change which files load. If your project keeps its assistant instructions in `AGENTS.md`, you can keep the snippet there and import that file from a `CLAUDE.md` beside it with an `@AGENTS.md` line ([share one file with other coding tools](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#share-one-file-with-other-coding-tools)). Claude Code can also read `AGENTS.md` directly, when there is no `CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` in the working directory or above it, in supported sessions; the [AGENTS.md section](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#agents-md) of the memory page gives the versions, settings and sessions in which it does.

tasks.title: Secure or audit this project
tasks.prompt: Secure this project using the guides at https://github.com/jposluns/secureconfig (see https://secureconfig.ai). Audit it first: list every listening service with its TLS and authentication state, and report the gaps as a table. Propose the fix for each gap per the matching guide (TLS on every endpoint, strong authentication, MFA where viable, and no secrets in the repository) and wait for my approval before changing anything. After approval, apply the fixes, run the README verification checklist, and report anything you could not test.

tasks.title: Review the AI and agent stack
tasks.prompt: Review the deployment exposure of this project's AI and agent infrastructure using the guides at https://github.com/jposluns/secureconfig (see https://secureconfig.ai). Inventory every AI-related service present: model servers, inference proxies, vector databases, MCP servers, agent builders, chat and image-generation UIs, notebooks, workflow tools, and observability services. Record each service's transport; for stdio MCP servers and other services with no network listener, mark bind address and TLS not applicable and instead review their inherited credentials and outbound access. For each, report its bind address, TLS state, authentication state, machine credentials, and outbound access to external services and cloud metadata; many of these tools need authentication configured and their defaults vary. Report the gaps as a table and propose the fix for each per the matching guide: loopback binding, a fronting TLS and login layer where there is no native control, scoped API keys, and egress control per egress-metadata.md. Wait for my approval before changing anything, then apply the fixes and run the README verification checklist. Keep the review within deployment exposure.

tasks.title: Audit for exposed business rules
tasks.prompt: Audit this project for confidential business rules exposed to the public, using the secret-handling guidance at https://github.com/jposluns/secureconfig (see https://secureconfig.ai), specifically secrets.md and web-exposure.md. A confidential pricing formula, allocation rule, or customer-specific process is protected because it is confidential, not because it is code, so treat it like a secret. Search these three exposure paths: the public repository and its git history, anything that ships to the browser (a NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ value, logic in client-shipped code, or a source map), and any prompt sent to a public LLM or an API outside your data agreement. Report each exposure as a table with its location and what it reveals, giving the exposure type rather than copying the confidential rule itself into the report. Propose the fix per secrets.md and web-exposure.md: move the rule into server-side code the client only calls, and keep it out of the client bundle and out of public LLM prompts. For anything already published, note that removal is hygiene, not containment, since it does not unpublish what was already public. Wait for my approval before changing anything, then apply the fixes and run the README verification checklist. Keep the review within deployment exposure.

tasks.title: Add single sign-on and MFA
tasks.prompt: Add single sign-on to this project using the guides at https://github.com/jposluns/secureconfig (see https://secureconfig.ai). Read identity-providers.md to choose between Google, Microsoft Entra, GitHub, or a hosted customer-identity provider that fits this project's users and budget, then wire it per oidc-integration.md: authorization code with PKCE, exact redirect URIs, token validation, and an allowlist check of the tenant, domain, or group so that a successful login is never treated as authorization. Enforce MFA at the provider, prefer passkeys for administrators, and run the README verification checklist before reporting completion.

tasks.title: Check your assistant against AIQT Guardrails
tasks.prompt: Assess this project, and the guardrails you yourself operate under, against the AIQT Guardrails standard at https://github.com/jposluns/guardrails (see https://aiqt.ai). Identify every gap: the accuracy, integrity, verification, and security behaviours the standard requires that this project or your current working rules do not yet meet. Recommend the specific guardrails to adopt, or adoption of the standard as a whole, with the reason for each recommendation.

tasks.title: Run a GRC gap assessment
tasks.prompt: Assess this project for governance, risk, compliance, and alignment to the standards covered by the GRC Library at https://github.com/jposluns/grc_library (see https://grclibrary.ai). Identify which of its domains and standards apply, deliver a gap assessment against each applicable control set, and provide either a prioritized improvement plan or an alignment register mapping the project's current state to the applicable controls.

description.text: {checks} checks to run before reporting completion, each with its command or method, and every result recorded as pass, fail, untested, or not applicable.
description.source: The home tile for this page ('with the command or method for each'); this page's meta ('Record each result as pass, fail, untested, or not applicable'); count from README.md Verification checklist

meta.text: Run the applicable checks and the Verify steps in every selected guide, in a fresh shell such as one started with `bash --norc --noprofile -i`. Replace `REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_HOST` with your own host before running anything. Record each result as pass, fail, untested, or not applicable, with evidence or a reason.

scope.text: The README marks every checklist item REASONED: each rests on its cited sources and records that it was not run against a deployment. Items 1 to 4 record local syntax checks and stub runs only. Item 8 names tools rather than a command and sets no pass threshold.

rule.text: Report a control as verified only for the checks that passed, and report every item you could not test instead of asserting that it passed.

rows.check: No plaintext listener on a public interface, except a listener whose only job is to redirect to HTTPS.
rows.quote: except a listener whose only job is to redirect to HTTPS

rows.check: Where HTTP is offered, the redirect works and carries a `Location: https://...` header.
Old protocols are refused: TLS 1.2 is the minimum. Confirm that the refusal came from the server and not from your own client.
rows.quote: Confirm the refusal came from the server and not from your own client

rows.check: An unauthenticated request to any non-public path returns 401, 403, or a login redirect, never data.
rows.method: The guarded anonymous probe in [oidc-integration.md](oidc-integration.md), once per non-public path
rows.quote: returns `401`, `403`, or a login redirect, never data

rows.check: No default credentials remain, and no secret is committed to the repository.
rows.method: `gitleaks git . && echo clean` for committed secrets; default accounts have no generic command, so check each service against its guide
rows.quote: Default accounts have no generic command: check each service against its guide

rows.check: Where ACME is used, renewal is automated, and something is actually scheduled to run it.
rows.method: `sudo certbot renew --dry-run --run-deploy-hooks`, then `sudo systemctl list-timers | grep -i certbot` or a `certbot renew` cron entry; for Caddy or Traefik, a completed renewal in their logs
rows.quote: Servers that manage renewal themselves (Caddy, Traefik) need no timer; confirm a completed renewal in their logs instead

rows.check: Public endpoints are scanned with the Qualys SSL Labs test or testssl.sh.
rows.method: [Qualys SSL Labs](https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/) or [testssl.sh](https://github.com/testssl/testssl.sh); no command and no pass threshold
rows.quote: names tools rather than a command and sets no pass threshold

rows.check: Human-facing logins carry a second factor where the stack supports one.
rows.method: An interactive login with only the password, attempting an MFA-protected operation
rows.quote: with only the password, attempt an MFA-protected operation

rows.check: Probed from outside the deployment network, from a second host, only the intended ports answer.
rows.method: The guarded `nmap -Pn -p-` block in [deployment-lifecycle.md](deployment-lifecycle.md), and its IPv6 companion, from a second host
rows.quote: only the intended ports may answer

rows.check: Where login comes from an identity provider, an identity outside the allowed tenant, domain, group, or users is denied.
rows.method: An interactive sign-in with an account outside the allowlist
rows.quote: an authenticated identity outside the allowed tenant, domain, group, or users is denied

entries.title: How the guides are sourced
entries.claim: The contribution rules require every configuration line, flag, or variable name in a guide to come from the vendor's documentation, with that page linked in the guide's dated Sources section. Where a tool has no native control, the guide says so and gives a fronting-layer pattern instead of inventing an option.
entries.limitation: Tracing each line to its source is an authoring and review duty. The guide-shape gate checks that a guide has a Verify section and dated Sources; it cannot check that a line matches the page it cites.

entries.title: What a Verify step rests on
entries.claim: Verify steps declare DEMONSTRATED, meaning the check ran against both the exposed and the fixed state, or REASONED, meaning it is derived from cited vendor behaviour. A reasoned step is never presented as verified.
entries.limitation: The marking gate checks that a declaration exists, not that the demonstration occurred or that the reasoning holds; that is checked in review. Older steps still being brought in line are listed in a baseline file.

entries.title: The verification checklist
entries.claim: The checklist sets out {checks} checks to run before reporting completion, with each result recorded as pass, fail, untested, or not applicable, and a control reported as verified only for the checks that passed.
entries.limitation: Every item is REASONED and records that it was not run against a deployment. Items 1 to 4 record local syntax checks and stub runs only, and item 8 names tools without a command or a pass threshold.

entries.title: Versions and dates
entries.claim: Most guides carry machine-readable front matter recording the sources checked and, where known, the exact versions. Guides date their sources in a section titled with the month and year they were checked; common-mistakes.md, a checklist that links to the fixes, carries none of its own.
entries.limitation: Versions are recorded where known; {versioned} of the {guides} guides are listed for the version-basis check. Vendor behaviour can change after the checked date.

entries.title: What the site loads
entries.claim: These pages load only files from this site: 3 stylesheets, the template's fonts, logos and marks, and 3 scripts: 1 reveals the copy buttons on 2 pages, 1 marks the section the reader is on in the contents list on 2 pages, and 1, on every page, shows the light and dark switch and applies the reader's choice. That script keeps the choice in the browser's local storage under the name scheme, only once the reader presses the switch, and sends nothing. The pages' own code sets no cookies, and the site's gates refuse inline script, inline style, and event-handler attributes in its pages.
entries.limitation: Cloudflare, which serves the site, can add its own scripts. The site's Content-Security-Policy allows Cloudflare's script and analytics hosts and inline scripts for its JavaScript Detections, by the owner's decision of 3 November 2026.

entries.title: Automated checks
entries.claim: Every gate in the suite is deterministic and offline, and the suite is the required status check on main. Every non-draft pull request runs the gates its changes affect, and a change to a guide, the code, the checks, a requirements file, a served script, the _headers file, a _redirects file or any site file of a type not on the content list runs the whole suite, so no change merges with a failing gate among those its changes affect. The whole suite also runs weekly.
entries.limitation: A change to a site file of a type on the content list (.html, .css, .json, .svg, .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .webp, .ico, .woff2, .txt and .xml: pages, page sources, stylesheets, fonts, images, text and XML files) that is not a requirements file, or to a project record, runs only the gates that read it; a requirements file runs the whole suite even with a listed suffix, and a gate a change does not run is checked in the next whole-suite run. The gates check the structure of the guides; whether a demonstration ran or a reasoned step is justified is checked in review. External links are swept weekly by an advisory job that does not block a merge.

label.source: This page's role: an unlisted security advisory for the maintainer

h1.text: n8n: a Code node that knows another execution's id may read its binary data (inference from a source review)
h1.source: finding-seed.out findings 1 and 7 and its proposal ('This guide infers'); finding-draft.out settled item 3 ('inferred from source; no run observed it')

status.text: This is a source-code review finding in n8n 2.40.6, not an executed exploit. Nothing from n8n was built or run. Every statement below about n8n's code or behaviour is either observed in source, carrying a file and line citation at commit 024ee46bdc6d57e5c47ef2c26bcac2b3a9efd827 (the n8n 2.40.6 tag) or, in Affected versions, at the n8n 2.47.2 tag, or labelled as inference.
status.source: finding-seed.out header ('Nothing from n8n was run') and finding 8; finding-draft.out ('nothing was built or run'); seed-n8n-binary/commits.txt

intro.text: The facts come only from the finding pack: its source review of n8n 2.40.6 at that commit, and its by-reading comparison of three files at n8n 2.47.2. This page carries the full read-path detail. It is reachable only by its own URL, and no other page on this site links it.
intro.source: finding-seed.out findings 1 to 8; the maintainer's instruction that the advisory is unlisted

report_title.text: Inference from a source review of n8n 2.40.6, not observed in a run: a JavaScript Code node task that already knows another workflow execution's id may read that execution's binary data, because no layer on the path checks that a caller-built binary-data id belongs to the running workflow or execution. Inference: where execution data is stored in `filesystem`, `s3` or `azure` mode and that store shares one root, bucket or container with the binary store, such a task that knows the workflow and execution ids may also read that execution's whole bundle.
report_title.source: finding-seed.out findings 1, 5 and 7 and its proposal; finding-draft.out settled item 3 and Body ('In the filesystem case this holds while both stores share one root')

affected.text: n8n 2.40.6, reviewed at commit 024ee46bdc6d57e5c47ef2c26bcac2b3a9efd827. Nothing was run.

Observed by reading only, at the n8n 2.47.2 tag (commit 626a58e55ccc2078dfc7a32486c09134fd059fa3), three of the reviewed files; the pack made no mechanical diff and did not check its 2.47.2 SHA256SUMS. At 2.47.2, `packages/core/src/binary-data/binary-data.service.ts` lines 133 to 159 match 2.40.6, including 141 to 143, and only `deleteMany` changed (2.47.2 lines 161 to 189).
affected.source: finding-seed.out finding 8 and Unsettled ('2.47.2 comparison limits'); seed-n8n-binary/commits.txt line 2

affected.text: At 2.47.2, `packages/core/src/binary-data/blob.manager.ts` has the same `getAsBuffer` body at lines 67 to 71, with only deletion handling changed (2.47.2 lines 14 to 15 and 195 to 225), and `packages/core/src/execution-engine/node-execution-context/utils/binary-helper-functions.ts` lines 1 to 237 read the same, including 128 to 153 and 137 to 138.

Inference: the read behaviour in those three files is unchanged at 2.47.2. The runner, broker, requester and managers were not available at 2.47.2, so this advisory does not state their 2.47.2 behaviour.

locations.text: The `getBinaryDataBuffer` helper exposed to Code tasks (`packages/core/src/execution-engine/node-execution-context/execute-context.ts:101-108`; `packages/@n8n/task-runner/src/runner-types.ts:107-128`).
The binary-data service's id split and manager dispatch (`packages/core/src/binary-data/binary-data.service.ts:139-147, 283-289`).

The blob manager's read with no parsing (`packages/core/src/binary-data/blob.manager.ts:63-66`) and the database manager's lookup by `fileId` alone (`packages/cli/src/binary-data/database.manager.ts:66-73`).

observed.text: `getBinaryDataBuffer` is one of seven helper RPC methods exposed to Code user code (`packages/@n8n/task-runner/src/runner-types.ts:107-128`), bound to `makeRpcCall` (`packages/@n8n/task-runner/src/js-task-runner/js-task-runner.ts:589-607, 653`) and sent unchanged in a `runner:rpc` message (`packages/@n8n/task-runner/src/task-runner.ts:510-536`).
The broker checks only that the task exists, then forwards the message (`packages/cli/src/task-runners/task-broker/task-broker.service.ts:336-353`).

The requester checks that the job exists and the method is on its allow-list, converts serialized Buffers, then calls the method on the task's `executeFunctions` (`packages/cli/src/task-runners/task-managers/task-requester.ts:402-418, 444-452`), which is the Code node's own execution context (`packages/core/src/execution-engine/node-execution-context/base-execute-context.ts:429-433`).

`getBinaryDataBuffer(itemIndex, propertyName)` passes the argument through (`packages/core/src/execution-engine/node-execution-context/execute-context.ts:101-108`). Any object with `mimeType` plus `data` or `id` passes `isBinaryValue` (`packages/workflow/src/type-guards.ts:103-110`) and is used as given (`packages/core/src/execution-engine/node-execution-context/utils/binary-helper-functions.ts:137-138`).

The service splits the id on a colon and picks the manager by that prefix (`packages/core/src/binary-data/binary-data.service.ts:139-147, 283-289`), and the blob manager calls `byteStore.read(fileId)` with no parsing (`packages/core/src/binary-data/blob.manager.ts:63-66`). The `EXECUTION_PATH_MATCHER` and `parseFileId` checks in that file are used only for deletion (`packages/core/src/binary-data/blob.manager.ts:14, 93-110, 168-183`).
The database manager looks a row up by `fileId` alone, with no `sourceId` filter (`packages/cli/src/binary-data/database.manager.ts:66-73`).

Binary keys in the filesystem, s3 and azure managers are `workflows/<wf>/executions/<ex>/binary_data/<uuid v4>` (`packages/core/src/binary-data/blob.manager.ts:151-160`), and database ids are bare uuid v4 values (`packages/cli/src/binary-data/database.manager.ts:36`).

The filesystem manager is always created (`packages/core/src/binary-data/binary-data.service.ts:41-47`), the database manager always registered (`packages/cli/src/commands/base-command.ts:359-360`), and the s3 and azure managers registered whenever their store is configured (`packages/cli/src/commands/base-command.ts:426-448`).

`FsByteStore.read` resolves every key through `getAbsolutePath`, which refuses a key whose path relative to the resolved storage root is empty, absolute or starts with `..` (`packages/@n8n/blob-storage/src/fs-byte-store.ts:46-54, 101-113`).

`S3ByteStore.read` and `AzureByteStore.read` pass the key on unchanged (`packages/@n8n/blob-storage/src/s3-byte-store.ee.ts:21-28`; `packages/@n8n/blob-storage/src/azure-byte-store.ee.ts:24-31`). The S3 service sends it as the object key in the configured bucket (`packages/@n8n/blob-storage/src/object-store/object-store.service.ee.ts:157-166`), and the Azure service uses it as the blob name in the configured container (`packages/@n8n/blob-storage/src/azure-blob/azure-blob.service.ee.ts:32-48, 94-100`).

The editor's `GET /binary-data` handler rejects `..` segments, its comment noting that the reader resolves the whole path so traversal could read another execution's file (`packages/cli/src/controllers/binary-data.controller.ts:58-87`).

That handler also checks `workflow:read` access to the execution or workflow behind the id before it reads (`packages/cli/src/controllers/binary-data.controller.ts:30-35`; `packages/cli/src/binary-data/binary-data-access.service.ts:28-73`).
`N8N_EXECUTION_DATA_STORAGE_MODE` takes `database`, the default, or `filesystem`, `s3` or `azure`, tagged `db`, `fs`, `s3` and `az` (`packages/core/src/storage.config.ts:10-24`).

A new execution's data is written with the configured mode's tag (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-persistence.ts:103, 115-121`): to the database in `db` mode, and otherwise to the JSON store (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-persistence.ts:979-981`).

The JSON store writes each bundle, holding the execution's data, workflow snapshot and version id (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-persistence.ts:116-120`), at `workflows/<wf>/executions/<n>/execution_data/bundle.json` (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-data/execution-data-json-store.ts:16-28`; `packages/cli/src/executions/execution-data/constants.ts:5`).

That key adds no random part of its own, unlike a binary key's uuid v4: beside the workflow id it holds fixed strings and `<n>`, the execution row's database insert id converted to a string (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-persistence.ts:111-113`).
observed.source: finding-seed.out finding 7 ('with no uuid in the key'); the #1252 QA review (execution-persistence.ts:112)

observed.text: The `fs` JSON store is rooted at `StorageConfig.storagePath` (`packages/core/src/fs-byte-store.service.ts:14-16`; `packages/cli/src/executions/execution-data/execution-data-json-store.ts:16-18`). The binary filesystem store is rooted at `N8N_BINARY_DATA_STORAGE_PATH` or, when that is unset, the same `storagePath` (`packages/core/src/binary-data/binary-data.config.ts:50-59`; `packages/core/src/binary-data/binary-data.service.ts:41-46`).

The `s3` and `az` JSON stores are registered on the same `ObjectStoreService` and `AzureBlobService` instances that back the binary s3 and azure managers (`packages/cli/src/commands/base-command.ts:426-448, 461-489`).

A JS or Python Code task's output `binary` object is passed through unchanged (`packages/@n8n/task-runner/src/js-task-runner/js-task-runner.ts:445-454`; `packages/@n8n/task-runner-python/src/task_executor.py:389-390`), and the Code node's result check only requires `binary` to be an object (`packages/nodes-base/nodes/Code/result-validation.ts:48-58`).

inferred.text: Inference, from the layers cited above: no layer on the Code-node path checks that the id belongs to the current workflow or execution, and no layer above the byte store rejects `..` segments; in filesystem mode `FsByteStore` refuses only a key that resolves outside its root.
inferred.source: finding-seed.out finding 1 ('Result', 'of the n8n-side layers I read'); finding-draft.out settled item 1

inferred.text: Inference, from those layers and a search of the pack for `hasReadAccess` and `parseExecutionFileId`: neither of the editor's checks is reached from the Code-node path.

Inference: since the manager is picked by the id's own prefix, the prefix can select any registered manager, so no value of `N8N_DEFAULT_BINARY_DATA_MODE` by itself removes the filesystem or database read path.
Inference: `FsByteStore`'s check compares resolved path text with no realpath step, so a `..` that stays inside the root passes and symlinks are outside the check.

Inference: reaching another execution's binary file needs its full id, including a uuid v4, which would have to leak to the attacker; guessing a uuid v4 is not practical, and where such an id could leak was not established.
Inference: a task that already knows another execution's binary-data id can read that execution's binary file. No run observed this.
inferred.source: finding-seed.out findings 1 and 7 and its proposal

inferred.text: Inference: in `filesystem`, `s3` or `azure` execution-data mode, a task that knows another execution's workflow id and execution id could read that execution's whole `bundle.json` by passing its key with the matching manager prefix, while the execution-data store and the binary store share one root, bucket or container. No run observed this.
inferred.source: finding-draft.out settled item 3 and Body ('In the filesystem case this holds while both stores share one root')

inferred.text: Inference: with the default paths the two filesystem roots are the same; whether setting only `N8N_BINARY_DATA_STORAGE_PATH` gives two roots was not traced, so the filesystem bundle read is claimed only while both stores share one root.
Inference: the execution id in the bundle key is a database insert id, which may be sequential and so guessable; whether it is, and whether a workflow id is guessable, was not established.
inferred.source: the #1252 QA review; finding-seed.out Unsettled ('Where ids could leak from')

inferred.text: Inference: a later node in the same workflow that reads a binary property by name (`packages/core/src/execution-engine/node-execution-context/utils/binary-helper-functions.ts:139-140`) would read whatever id the Code node supplied.

steps.text: Read the JS Code-node RPC path from `getBinaryDataBuffer` through the broker and requester to the binary-data service and the blob or database manager, and confirm no layer ties the id to the running workflow or execution.
Confirm that the editor's `GET /binary-data` download ties the id to `workflow:read` access and rejects `..`, and that neither check is reached from the Code-node path.

Check the configured `N8N_EXECUTION_DATA_STORAGE_MODE`; in `filesystem`, `s3` or `azure` mode, check whether the execution-data store and the binary store share one root, bucket or container, and read how the bundle key is formed (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-data/execution-data-json-store.ts:20-28`).

Note, without running an exploit, which ids each read needs, from the binary and bundle key layouts cited above, and that the pack established neither where such ids could leak nor whether they can be guessed.

poc.text: None run. This is a source review; nothing from n8n was built or executed, and no read of another execution's data was observed. The impact below is inference from the source.

impact.text: Inference: a user who can create or edit a JavaScript Code node, and who already knows another execution's binary-data id, could read that execution's stored binary data. Inference: in `filesystem`, `s3` or `azure` execution-data mode, while the execution-data store and the binary store share one root, bucket or container, such a user who knows another execution's workflow id and execution id could read its whole `bundle.json`, which holds that execution's data and workflow snapshot. Confidentiality only; no write or denial of service is claimed. No run observed this.
impact.source: finding-seed.out finding 7; finding-draft.out settled item 3 and Body

cvss_vector.text: PROVISIONAL CVSS 4.0 vector for the worst case this page states, the bundle read: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`. It is provisional: it is not computed to a numeric score, it rests on source review with no run, and this page asserts no numeric severity.
cvss_vector.source: This advisory's assessment, labelled provisional; CVSS 4.0 vector metrics

cvss_derivation.text: Derivation of AT:P, from the inferences above: the bundle read needs a deployment condition the attacker does not control, a non-default `N8N_EXECUTION_DATA_STORAGE_MODE` whose store shares the binary store's root, bucket or container, and with that met its key needs only a workflow id and an execution id, whose guessability was not established. By the same inferences, the binary-file read needs a leaked uuid v4 key instead; whether CVSS 4.0 rates such a secret under AT:P or AC:H was not checked against the specification, which this review did not have, so that read's vector may differ. The other metrics: a network-reachable editor (AV:N); an authenticated user who can edit a Code node (PR:L); no other user's action and, by inference, no security-enhancing condition to evade on the path (UI:N, AC:L); another execution's data and workflow snapshot (VC:H); and no write, denial of service or subsequent-system impact claimed (VI:N, VA:N, SC:N, SI:N, SA:N).
cvss_derivation.source: This advisory's assessment from finding-seed.out findings 1, 5 and 7 and finding-draft.out settled item 3; the #1252 QA review

mitigations.text: Keep `N8N_EXECUTION_DATA_STORAGE_MODE` at its `database` default (`packages/core/src/storage.config.ts:18-20`), under which a new execution's data is written to the database, not the JSON store (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-persistence.ts:103, 979-981`). Inference: new bundles then do not reach the filesystem root, bucket or container that the binary managers read. The persistence class's comment says reads follow each execution's recorded `storedAt` value (`packages/cli/src/executions/execution-persistence.ts:61-64`). Inference: switching back to `database` leaves bundles already written in place.
mitigations.source: finding-draft.out Body ('keep N8N_EXECUTION_DATA_STORAGE_MODE at its database default'); n8n.md as merged in #1250 labels the switch-back as inference

mitigations.text: Where people you do not trust can edit workflows, exclude the Code node (`n8n-nodes-base.code`) with `NODES_EXCLUDE`. n8n's security audit lists the Code node among its official risky node types (`packages/cli/src/security-audit/constants.ts:51-53`) and recommends not loading unneeded node types with `NODES_EXCLUDE` (`packages/cli/src/security-audit/risk-reporters/nodes-risk-reporter.ts:48-58`). Inference: AI Transform and Code Tool tasks may get the same RPC helpers, so excluding the Code node alone may not close the path. No setting limiting who can edit Code nodes was read.
mitigations.source: finding-draft.out Body ('NODES_EXCLUDE'); n8n.md as merged in #1250 gives the same advice
